0.0.n: さん makes this way of addressing the audience polite.

0.1.n: This standard daytime greeting is written with は at the end, pronounced わ.

0.3.n: Combines with 教師 to specify the language she teaches.

0.4.n: This is a job title, used here to describe her own profession.

0.5.n: の links her job title to her name; it does not express ownership here.

0.6.n: This is the speaker’s name, not the ordinary word for future.

0.7.n: A polite sentence ending; the speaker leaves out 私, meaning I.

1.0.n: Read きょう here; it sets the time for the practice.

1.1.n: は marks 今日 as the topic, framing what they will do today.

1.2.n: Pairs with に to describe doing the practice with someone else.

1.3.n: に turns 一緒 into an expression describing how they will practice.

1.5.n: Names the situation in which the Japanese expressions will be useful.

1.6.n: で marks travel as the setting where the expressions are useful.

1.7.n: This plain verb form describes 日本語 in the next line.

2.0.n: Combines with 機関 to form 交通機関, referring to transport services or means.

2.1.n: Part of 交通機関, which includes transportation such as trains and buses.

2.2.n: で marks transportation as the setting where the Japanese is used.

2.3.n: This plain verb form directly describes 日本語: Japanese that you use.

2.4.n: Both 役立つ and 使う describe the Japanese they will practice.

2.5.n: を marks 日本語 as what they will practice.

2.6.n: 練習する becomes 練習しましょう, a polite invitation to practice together.

0.lit: Everyone, hello; Japanese-language teacher Mirai am.
0.tip: Job title + の + name is a common pattern for introducing yourself.

1.lit: Today, as for, together, during travel useful...
1.tip: The sentence continues into the next line: 役立つ describes the Japanese they will practice.

2.lit: Transportation on use Japanese-language object let’s practice.
2.tip: 使う comes before 日本語 to mean Japanese that you use, without a separate word for that.
